title: Waiver-Funded Home Modification Back Office and Factoring
one_liner: Handle the prior-authorization paperwork and advance payment for small contractors who do ramps and bathroom retrofits funded by Medicaid waivers and VA grants.
customer: Small accessibility and remodeling contractors (3-15 employees) in states with waiver home-modification benefits, plus case managers and AAAs who can't find bidders.
problem: Senior housing supply is stuck through 2030, so aging in place is structurally favored and home mods are the cheapest fix. But waiver and VA HISA funding needs OT assessments, multiple bids, packets, inspections and 60-120 day payment, so good contractors avoid it. Approved seniors can't find anyone to do the work.
solution: A back office that prepares the packet (OT evaluation scheduling, standard scope, photos, bids, permits), tracks approval, submits invoices, and advances 85-90% of payment within five days against the approved authorization. A network directory shows case managers which contractors are ready to bid.
why_now: 41 states have HCBS waitlists over 600k, so states favor cheap home-based solutions over $115k-a-year nursing home stays. Medicaid cuts and 15-month waits add pressure, while 80+ growth means demand for mods is up.
revenue_model: 3-5% packet fee, a 1.5-3% factoring spread, and a platform fee from states or MCOs for a ready-to-bid contractor pool.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for funded home modifications is contractor cash flow and paperwork, not consumer demand or budget. Fixing the contractor's experience creates supply where the money already exists.
first_30_days: In one state, recruit five contractors and process 10 packets. Secure a small credit line from a CDFI or SBA lender to fund advances, then approach the state's HCBS case management office.

title: Lender-Required Benefit Records for F&I Add-Ons
one_liner: A 20-second, VIN-aware 'did this product actually benefit this buyer' check and signed record that indirect lenders demand as a funding stip, because California's CARS Act (SB 766) bans add-ons that provide no benefit and lenders inherit the exposure.
customer: Primary payer: credit unions and banks that buy indirect auto paper in California (dealer-management and compliance teams). Secondary: California franchised and independent dealer groups, at about $149 per store per month, when a lender tells them to use it.
problem: SB 766 becomes operative Oct 1, 2026. It bars charging for an add-on the buyer would not benefit from, requires clear disclosure that add-ons are optional, and requires dealers to keep records for two years. Lenders that buy the contracts carry Holder Rule and Rees-Levering exposure for what happens in the F&I office. Nobody outside the dealership can see whether GAP was sold to a buyer with 35% down, a 7-year service contract to a buyer with 6 years of factory powertrain warranty left, or prepaid oil changes to an EV buyer. The FTC's federal CARS Rule was vacated in January 2025, so states and private plaintiffs are the enforcement, and the April 2026 $78.1M Lindsay Automotive settlement shows the size of the downside.
solution: A lightweight web form and API that the F&I manager fills in per product during the menu. It auto-decodes the VIN (EV or hybrid, remaining factory warranty, tire type, key type). It pulls loan-to-value from the deal numbers and runs benefit rules per product, such as GAP with LTV under about 90%, a service contract that overlaps the factory warranty, maintenance on an EV, and key replacement on a keyless-start car. It flags mismatches, captures a one-tap 'customer chose this anyway, here's why' rationale, and outputs a timestamped PDF and JSON record. Lenders add it to their funding-package checklist. The rule library is the product and is updated per state as CARS-style bills spread.
why_now: SB 766 takes effect in three days (Oct 1, 2026). Federal rule-making is dead, so the compliance burden has moved to states and to lenders' third-party-risk teams. More states are copying California's language. The Lindsay $78.1M settlement in April 2026 made every dealer compliance director and every credit union counsel pay attention.
revenue_model: Per-funded-contract fee of $2 to $4 paid by the lender or passed to the dealer, or a $149 per store per month dealer subscription. Later, sell state-by-state rule packs and an anonymized benefit-mismatch benchmark to lenders and dealer insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Most dealer violations are not lies. They are menu autopilot. The DMS menu shows the same five products on every deal and the pay plan rewards penetration, so a mismatch happens without anyone deciding to deceive. The buyer who will pay for compliance is not the dealer, whose incentive is to sell. It is the lender, who holds the paper, gets sued alongside the dealer, and has the leverage to make a data field mandatory at funding.
first_30_days: Read the SB 766 text and the FTC's vacated rule for the exact 'no benefit' examples, and turn them into 25 to 30 explicit rules. Build a plain web form with no DMS integration. Cold-pitch compliance officers at 15 California credit unions with big indirect books through the CUNA/California credit union compliance channels. Offer a free 60-day pilot in which they require it from their 3 to 5 highest-volume dealers. Pre-sell 10 dealers at $99 per month using the line 'your lender is going to ask for this.'

title: Collective Anti-Piracy Desk for 3D-Print Miniature Creators
one_liner: A creator-owned enforcement collective that fingerprints STL/3D-print models, hunts leaks across Telegram, Discord and marketplaces, and uses EU Digital Services Act notice, trusted-flagger and appeal rights to make takedowns stick.
customer: Independent sculptors and small studios selling printable miniatures, terrain and tabletop models via Patreon, Kickstarter, MyMiniFactory, Cults3D and their own stores (tens of thousands worldwide, top creators earning six figures). Also indie designers of other collectible models (keyboard cases, cosplay props) and the hosting platforms that want a clean enforcement feed.
problem: Files leak within days of release, spread through Discord and Telegram, get resold on Etsy/eBay/Temu-style marketplaces and printed into physical minis. A solo creator faces hundreds of infringements a month, and one-by-one DMCA notices cost hours, are ignored or are countered by repeat offenders. Brand-protection vendors price for brands, not solo sculptors. The EU Digital Services Act gave structured levers (Art. 16 notice-and-action, Art. 17 statements of reasons, Art. 21 out-of-court dispute bodies, Art. 22 trusted-flagger priority) and put very large marketplaces such as Temu and AliExpress under Commission supervision, but nobody has packaged these levers for small creators.
solution: (1) Geometry-based mesh fingerprinting, robust to re-meshing, scaling, splitting and hollowing, plus image similarity for renders and prints, with crawlers for leak channels, marketplaces and cloud-drive links. (2) A case engine that files DMCA and DSA notices in correct legal form, tracks counter-notices and statements of reasons, and escalates repeat infringers to the platform's regulator complaint channels. (3) An EU-established entity built to apply for DSA trusted-flagger status; Art. 22 explicitly favors bodies that represent collective interests and are independent of platforms. (4) A 'legit copy' program that offers print farms and Etsy resellers a licensed route, so leaks become royalty income.
why_now: The printable-model economy on Patreon and 3D-printer adoption are at scale. The DSA has been fully applicable since Feb 2024 and the Commission's 2025 actions against Temu/AliExpress make regulator escalation credible (verify status). AI re-meshing and generative 3D tools make exact-hash detection obsolete. Pressure from IP owners like Games Workshop pushes hobbyists toward original designs, so creator-owned IP is growing.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $29-149/month by catalog size. 10-20% share of licensed royalties recovered from converted resellers. Enterprise feed for hosting platforms that want a vetted trusted-flagger channel.
non_obvious_insight: Piracy at this scale is a coordination problem. Thirty thousand creators each losing $5-50k cannot afford lawyers, but as a collective with formal DSA status they generate volume and quality that platforms must prioritise. The realistic prize is converting pirates into licensees (print farms reselling legally), not just takedown counts.
first_30_days: Sign 10 mid-tier Patreon sculptors for a free 30-day leak report. Build the fingerprint and crawler MVP with open-source mesh-hashing plus CLIP embeddings. Send DMCA/DSA notices through a part-time attorney and measure takedown rates. Convert reports to $49/month subscriptions. Register the EU entity and start the trusted-flagger application with counsel.

title: Install Clubs: Brazilian Consórcio for Home Contractors
one_liner: A contractor-anchored, interest-free buying pool: 60-200 homeowners pay monthly into escrow and each month a few move up the queue (by draw or bid) to get their roof, heat pump or solar+battery installed.
customer: Independent home-service contractors (roofing, HVAC/heat pump, solar+storage, windows) with 5-50 staff who want pre-sold backlog. Their end users are homeowners who have been quoted $8-20k and don't want a 9-12% HELOC or home-improvement loan.
problem: Big-ticket home upgrades stall on financing. Contractors burn 10-20% of revenue on lead gen and lose many quoted jobs because the homeowner can't or won't borrow. The 25C/25D federal credits ended for installs after Dec 31, 2025, so the effective price jumped overnight.
solution: Software + bank escrow + a lawyer-drafted prepaid-service template that lets a contractor run a 'club' for one product (e.g., a $9k heat-pump install). Members pay $100-200/month into segregated escrow. Every month one or more members are allocated an install by lottery or by bidding extra to jump the queue. The contractor is the counterparty and delivers at a locked price, so there is no loan and no interest. The platform earns an administration fee instead of interest, as Brazilian consórcios do.
why_now: Brazil's consórcio system hit a record 12.76M active participants and about R$500B of credit sold in 2025, in a high-rate environment, so the model is proven when loans are expensive. In the US the 25C/25D credits vanished on Dec 31, 2025, rates are still high, and the only consórcio-style player I found (NWX) sells general credit letters for real estate and vehicles. Nobody has wrapped the pool around a service the seller delivers.
revenue_model: Administration fee of roughly 8-12% of contract value collected in monthly installments, a SaaS fee per contractor club, and a share of escrow float yield.
non_obvious_insight: A consórcio is not a loan, it is a queue with a price guarantee. Making the licensed contractor the counterparty turns the pool into a prepaid-service escrow (like layaway) instead of a credit product, which sidesteps most lending regulation. The contractor gets what it wants most: scheduled backlog, cash before work, and near-zero CAC because 'your neighbor's roof gets done this month' recruits the next member. Homeowners who were declined or scared off by loans are the fastest-filling segment.
first_30_days: Sign 2-3 contractors in one state. Get an escrow account at a community bank and a prepaid-service agreement drafted by a lawyer who knows that state's home-improvement deposit rules. Mine each contractor's list of past quotes that never closed and pre-enroll about 40 members in a 'Founders Club' at about $150/month for a $9k install. Run the first allocation in month 2, so the first installed job and first admin-fee revenue land by around day 60.

title: Evac Cash: Payout When Ordered to Evacuate
one_liner: A few dollars a month buys a $500-$2,500 wire within hours of an official mandatory evacuation order for your address, covering hurricane, wildfire and burn-scar flood orders.
customer: Renters and lower-to-middle-income homeowners in evacuation zones: Gulf and Florida surge zones, Western wildfire-urban-interface neighborhoods, and LA burn-scar areas. Sold to individuals, through employers of hourly staff (hospitals, hotels, nursing homes, grocers), and through credit unions or municipal 'evac funds'.
problem: Evacuating costs $1,000-$3,000 (gas, hotel, lost shifts, pet boarding) and the money is needed before any claim exists. Cost is a common reason people stay, so the people most exposed are least able to leave. Civil-authority and additional-living-expense cover is slow, receipt-based, often conditional on nearby damage, and many renters lack it.
solution: A parametric contract whose trigger is a legal act. If your geocoded address sits inside a polygon under a mandatory evacuation order, or an NWS flash-flood emergency for a burn scar, the platform pays via FedNow/RTP or a push-to-card within hours. Zone data comes from county emergency-management systems (evacuation-zone platforms and state zone maps). Tiers are priced by zone frequency, with one payout per event per address and a simple app that alerts you and shows your zone. Underwritten via a licensed MGA and fronting carrier, first as employer group policies.
why_now: Address-level, machine-readable evacuation zones are now common. FedNow/RTP make hours-not-weeks payouts cheap. The LA fires of January 2025 made burn-scar exposure vivid, and NOAA CPC/IRI's September 2026 outlooks show a greater than 90% chance of a very strong El Niño this winter, which means heavy rain on fresh burn scars and flash-flood/debris-flow evacuation orders. Parametric reinsurance capacity is plentiful and MGAs want small-ticket distribution.
revenue_model: Premium of roughly $3-$15 per month depending on how often each zone is ordered out (about 1.3-1.5x expected payout), or $1-$3 per employee per month on group plans. The company keeps an MGA commission of 15-25%, plus municipal, nonprofit and employer-funded policies for vulnerable residents. Later it can sell zone-frequency data to emergency managers.
non_obvious_insight: The best parametric trigger is a legal act, not a physical measurement. An evacuation order is binary, public, address-specific and timestamped, so basis risk nearly vanishes. Paying people to leave also changes behavior and saves lives, which makes employers and governments willing co-payers, so the product has two buyers instead of one.
first_30_days: Sign a parametric MGA and fronting carrier. Build the polygon match and instant-payout flow on public evacuation-zone data. Pilot a group policy for about 200 hourly workers at one Gulf hospital or hotel employer and one credit union serving a LA burn-scar community. Offer emergency-management agencies a free 'what zone am I in' tool for distribution. Goal: 500 covered addresses before peak rain season.

title: Neutral Caninization Platform for Pet Antibody Drugs
one_liner: A species-adaptation and developability service that lets animal-health companies without Zoetis's proprietary platform make dog, cat and horse antibody drugs.
customer: Mid-size animal-health companies (Elanco, Boehringer Ingelheim Animal Health, Merck Animal Health, Dechra, Ceva, Virbac, Asian vet-pharma) and pet-biotech startups.
problem: Companion-animal mAbs (Cytopoint, Librela, Solensia, Lenivia, Portela) are dominated by one player with roughly 85-90% of revenue, built on a proprietary caninization platform. Others cannot reliably turn a validated human target into a dog- or cat-ready antibody with proper Fc biology, FcRn-driven half-life and low anti-drug-antibody risk. AI binder-design tools are trained on human and mouse data, not canine or feline.
solution: Offer (1) canine, feline and equine germline-framework and Fc libraries with species-specific FcRn and FcgR binding assays, (2) AI-assisted binder design and caninization against validated pet targets (IL-31, NGF, IL-4/13, CD20, PD-1), (3) canine PBMC and ADA-risk screens, and (4) a lead plus data package for USDA or FDA-CVM pathways. Sell as fixed-price programs.
why_now: 2026 review literature names species adaptation and Fc biology as the missing platform pieces. Zero-shot AI antibody design has reached double-digit hit rates, so making binders is cheap while species adaptation is the moat. Zoetis's pet-mAb franchise proves the commercial size, and FDA's expanded conditional approval for major species (through 2028) is available.
revenue_model: $150-400k per program plus milestones and deliberately light royalties, and reagent sales (species-specific FcRn and receptor kits).
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume AI-designed drugs must prove themselves in human oncology. Animal health has smaller and faster trials, direct-pay owners and a concentrated incumbent whose moat is the platform, not the targets. AI attacks exactly that platform. The first AI-designed antibody drug on the market may well be for dogs.
first_30_days: Build canine and feline framework and Fc reagent sets from public sequences and gene synthesis (~$20k). Run FcRn binding on 10 published veterinary mAbs to show calibration. Pitch 15 animal-health BD leads and 5 pet-biotech startups. Sign 1-2 paid feasibility studies ($30-60k), such as caninizing a validated human target.

title: SLA-Backed Mirror of At-Risk Public Earth Data
one_liner: A paid continuity service that keeps free federal Earth-observation feeds flowing, with bridge products and an SLA, when the originals degrade or go dark.
customer: Crop and weather insurers, commodity and energy trading desks, hydropower and utilities, and reinsurers whose models ingest free NOAA, NASA and USGS satellite products.
problem: Free satellite and climate feeds have no SLA. Since 2025, reported budget pressure and retirements (DMSP-derived products, some NOAA archives) and aging flagship sensors (MODIS-era platforms nearing end of life) have exposed downstream firms to a single point of failure they never underwrote.
solution: A 'Data Continuity Desk': mirror the top 50 at-risk feeds, cross-calibrate substitutes (VIIRS, Sentinel-3, Landsat, commercial sensors) into documented bridge products, alert on schema and quality changes, and contractually guarantee delivery. Add an audit that maps each customer's model to its data dependencies.
why_now: The briefing notes NOAA and NASA EO budget cuts were not covered, so treat specifics as unverified. Prior knowledge points to 2025-26 funding fights and curtailed products. Meanwhile Sentinel and commercial sensors are mature enough to serve as bridges.
revenue_model: $2-50k per year per data product under SLA. $15-40k for a dependency audit. Enterprise bundles for insurers and trading desks.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders think free public data is a permanent public good. The businesses built on it hold an uninsured operational risk, and the seller who quantifies that risk and guarantees continuity gets paid like an insurer.
first_30_days: Inventory the 100 most cited NOAA, NASA and USGS feeds and score each for discontinuation risk. Publish the list, then call 30 insurers and trading desks and ask which feeds they run on. Build one bridge product, for example a snow or vegetation index, and sign two paid pilots.

title: Age Assurance Kit for Small Game Communities
one_liner: A drop-in age-gating kit that never stores IDs, with regulator-ready audit trails, for indie multiplayer studios, mod sites, fan forums and Minecraft-style server networks.
customer: Indie multiplayer studios (5-100 staff) with in-game chat, modding and fan-wiki sites, forums, and server networks selling ranks, mainly in the UK and EU.
problem: The UK Online Safety Act enforcement deadline was 2025-07-25, and Discord announced mandatory face-scan or ID checks worldwide in March 2026. Discord's Sept 2025 breach was claimed to have exposed 2.1M ID photos, and photo checks were beaten with Death Stranding character images. Small operators have mandates with no compliance budget.
solution: An SDK and plugin set (Unity, Unreal, Discord bot, Discourse, WordPress, Minecraft servers) that routes each user through the cheapest sufficient method (on-device estimation, card check, reusable wallet attestations). It stores only a signed over-13 or over-18 token, and ships risk-assessment templates and audit logs.
why_now: Enforcement is live, the Roblox and Discord rollouts set user expectations, and a leaked-ID breach makes 'we never hold your ID' a selling point.
revenue_model: $29-199 per month per community plus $0.02-0.10 per verification, with a documentation package for regulators.
non_obvious_insight: Large vendors sell to big platforms, but the long tail needs self-serve pricing and paperwork, not just a verification call. The liability is holding the ID, so a token-only design is the product, not a feature.
first_30_days: Ship a Discord bot and WordPress plugin on top of an existing estimation and wallet vendor. Recruit 20 forum and server operators through modding and Minecraft communities. Convert 5 to paid plans and write the regulator documentation pack.

title: Broker Spread Reveal: Two-Sided Freight Ledger
one_liner: Match what shippers paid brokers against what carriers were actually paid, so every broker's true margin by lane becomes visible for the first time.
customer: Mid-market shippers with $20M to $300M in annual freight spend, using 2 to 6 brokers with no real audit, including PE-owned manufacturers and distributors. Secondary buyers are owner-operators and small carriers at $19 to $49 a month, and freight-procurement consultancies.
problem: Each side holds half the ledger. The shipper knows what it paid the broker. The carrier knows what the broker paid it, on the rate confirmation in the glovebox. The broker's spread, commonly 10 to 35%, stays invisible. Freight-audit firms check invoices against contract rates but never see the carrier payout. 49 CFR 371.3 already requires brokers to keep records of shipper rate, carrier rate and margin. The 2024 proposal to require electronic records and a 48-hour response had still not been finalized as of 2026 status reports. Individual drivers who ask for the record get ghosted.
solution: Carriers text or email a photo of each rate confirmation to a bot. Claude vision extracts lane, dates, load number, broker and pay. Shippers upload freight invoices or a TMS export. The engine pairs the two by load number, origin and destination, and date, then produces a shipper dashboard: 'You paid $412K, carriers received $331K, effective broker take 19.6%. Broker A averages 12% on Chicago to Atlanta, Broker B 27%.' It also generates ready-to-send 371.3 record requests. Aggregated, anonymized carrier-side data becomes a 'Broker Take Index' by lane, giving shippers a benchmark for re-bidding and giving carriers a list of which brokers keep the most.
why_now: The pending 2024 rulemaking has put broker margin disclosure on every carrier's and shipper's radar. The Montgomery ruling has brokers on the defensive. Soft freight markets in 2025 to 2026 have shippers squeezing logistics spend. Vision-model OCR now makes ratecon parsing nearly free, where it would have needed a data-entry team three years ago.
revenue_model: Shipper SaaS at $1.5k to $6k a month, or 10 to 15% of first-year savings after a re-bid. Owner-operators freemium, with $19 a month for lane-level broker-take data. Anonymized benchmark reports to procurement consultancies and private-equity operating partners.
non_obvious_insight: The freight-audit industry is blind to carrier payout because it is the broker's proprietary secret. Only drivers hold the other half, as ratecon photos on their phones. Individual carriers who invoke 371.3 get ghosted, but a shipper with contractual audit rights gets an answer, and shippers are the ones who can pay. Drivers are free supply, shippers are paying demand, and neither can build this alone. Handle rate-confirmation confidentiality clauses by publishing only anonymized aggregates and letting shippers request records under their own audit rights.
first_30_days: Build a ratecon email and SMS intake bot in about a week. Seed it with 100 owner-operators from OOIDA-style Facebook groups by offering a free 'your rate vs. lane average' check. Collect 2,000 ratecons in the first month. Through freight consultants and PE operating partners, offer 10 mid-size shippers a free one-lane spread report built from their last 12 months of invoices plus the crowd data. Convert the first 2 to 3 to a $2k a month pilot.

title: Babel Tables for Multilingual Community Programs
one_liner: A tabletop translation hub that lets a senior-center lunch, ESL class or church group hold one conversation across four languages in real time.
customer: Senior centers, Area Agencies on Aging, libraries, faith groups and community colleges in multilingual cities, paying $150-300 a month per site plus hardware, funded from language-access and aging-services budgets.
problem: More than 25 million Americans have limited English proficiency, and isolated immigrant elders sit in language-siloed programs or nowhere. Interpreters cost $60-120 an hour, so programming stays segregated by language, blocking intergenerational and cross-cultural ties. Asian adults were the only Pew group net positive on chatbots for loneliness (37% help, 25% hurt), which signals openness to tech-mediated connection.
solution: A 4-microphone puck plus tablet that separates speakers and streams speech-to-speech translation to earbuds or phones, and captions on a table screen, for up to four languages at once. 'Table mode' runs low-stakes conversation card games, 'host mode' supports classes. Audio is processed ephemerally, with a human interpreter fallback for high-stakes moments.
why_now: Speech-to-speech translation reached conversational latency and usable quality in 2025 (translation in earbuds and meeting platforms), and small on-device models make private processing possible. State and city language-access mandates persist. Loneliness is a WHO-measured metric.
revenue_model: Hardware plus per-site SaaS, per-language add-ons, and contracts with city aging departments and Area Agencies on Aging.
non_obvious_insight: Translation tech was sold as an accommodation for one person and one interpreter. The bigger use is mixing: making the group itself multilingual so a Cantonese widow, a Spanish-speaking teen volunteer and an English-speaking regular can share one table. The unit of value is the table, not the user.
first_30_days: Prototype with a $200 speakerphone and a phone app. Pilot 'Table Tuesdays' in two senior centers (Chinese, Spanish, English) through a city aging department. Collect participation data over four weeks and charge $99 a month.

title: Get Paid to Care: Family Caregiver Enrollment
one_liner: A navigator that gets family caregivers onto Medicaid and VA payrolls, then becomes the fiscal intermediary that pays them.
customer: Adult children and spouses (45-70) giving 20+ hours a week of unpaid care to a low-income parent or veteran. Secondary buyers are Area Agencies on Aging, Medicaid managed-care plans and state Medicaid agencies that pay fiscal-intermediary fees.
problem: 59M family caregivers gave 49.5B unpaid hours in 2024 (about $1T) and lose roughly $21k a year in income. Every state has Medicaid self-direction, many pay relatives, and the VA has Veteran-Directed Care. But the rules differ by state, the assessment sets the hours, and agencies and fiscal intermediaries earn more by placing an outside aide.
solution: Phase 1 is a state-by-state 'can I get paid?' screener plus done-with-you enrollment: eligibility, application packet, coaching for the nurse assessment (which sets hours), employee onboarding, timesheet and electronic-visit-verification coaching, and appeals. Phase 2 is to become a licensed fiscal intermediary (payroll, background checks, EVV) in states that allow several vendors, and to bill the state a monthly per-participant fee.
why_now: About $911B in federal Medicaid cuts plus work requirements, 41 states with HCBS waitlists over 600k people (average wait 15 months), and Wisconsin agencies 'not able to take new clients' after the 2026 visa and TPS shocks. States now have to lean on the caregiver already in the house.
revenue_model: Families pay a flat $349-499 per successful enrollment, or a lower fee plus a first-year success fee. Phase 2 adds state or MCO fiscal-intermediary per-member-per-month fees. AAAs can pay for referral-sourced enrollment.
non_obvious_insight: The shortage is partly a payment-eligibility problem, not a bodies problem. The gatekeepers who could help families avoid agencies are the agencies and legacy fiscal intermediaries, so no one with a business incentive teaches families the paid-relative pathway.
first_30_days: Pick two states where relatives can be paid and enrollment is open (California's IHSS is the obvious one). Publish the screener and state guides, then capture leads through caregiver support groups, Facebook groups and elder-law firms. Sell a $349 concierge enrollment to the first 20 families and measure approval rate and approved hours.

title: Lot-Level Verification for Generic Semaglutide Importers
one_liner: A shared-API lineage database plus independent identity and impurity testing for distributors and pharmacy chains buying the flood of post-patent generic semaglutide.
customer: Distributors, pharmacy chains, hospital groups and telehealth clinics in India, Canada, Brazil and the 75+ markets Indian exporters like Hetero now target, and payers or regulators who need lot-level evidence.
problem: Semaglutide patents lapsed in Canada (Jan 2026), India and Brazil (Mar 2026), and 40+ Indian companies launched brands within weeks. By July, Dr. Reddy's halted supply through at least late October over an API impurity, and Torrent recalled Semalix batches after Dr. Reddy's notice because it uses the same API. Buyers can't see which brands share which API source, and fake pens circulate.
solution: Build an API-lineage graph from customs and shipping records, regulatory notices, recalls and public dossiers, mapping each brand and batch to its API manufacturer, and alert subscribers when any brand in the shared-API cluster has an event. Pair this with fast lot testing (LC-MS peptide identity and purity, impurity profile) through accredited partner labs in India, the UAE and Brazil, returning a signed 'verified lot' certificate with QR lookup. Start with a free public recall-radar page and newsletter to collect buyers.
why_now: Generics launched in March-July 2026 across three large markets at once (India prices as low as Rs 1,500 a month), regulators are stretched, and the first recalls and counterfeit guidance are already published. Tirzepatide and US semaglutide remain patented, so the gray market will keep growing alongside the legitimate one.
revenue_model: $250-$600 per verified lot, $500-$2,000 a month for lineage alerts and API access, and custom supplier audits for hospital groups and exporters.
non_obvious_insight: Forty-plus brands is not forty-plus independent risks: a handful of API sources means one impurity event propagates across supposedly competing brands, and no buyer-side tool maps that. Evidence: BusinessLine's headline 'DRL's semaglutide supply hits a stumbling block, affects other companies too' and Economic Times' Torrent recall after Dr. Reddy's notice (Jul 9, 2026) via Google News (https://news.google.com/rss/search?q=Torrent+Semalix+recall+Dr+Reddy%27s+API+semaglutide+Canada); Fierce Pharma on the pause (https://www.fiercepharma.com/manufacturing/dr-reddys-presses-pause-generic-semaglutide-supply-after-flagging-api-issue). India Today: 'Quality concerns hit cheap Ozempic copies in India within months'. NDTV, Mar 30, 2026: 'How To Spot Fakes'. Hetero: 1.5M pens, 75+ markets (Medical Dialogues Apr 16, 2026). Patent-expiry dates and 40-50 brands: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semaglutide.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: assemble a public database of every Indian semaglutide brand, the marketing-authorization holder, contract manufacturer and any disclosed API source, and ship the recall-radar page. Days 7-20: sign a testing-lab partner in India or the UAE on a wholesale per-lot price, and run 20 lots bought retail as a published 'state of the market' report. Days 20-30: pitch 25 importers, pharmacy chains and telehealth clinics with a free lineage check plus a $400 lot test, and aim for 5 paid tests.

title: Fractional Operator for Tiny Private Water Systems
one_liner: A flat-fee compliance back office and operator-of-record for the mobile-home parks, small subdivisions and rural employers that own small water systems and are about to face PFAS testing in 2027.
customer: Owners of mobile-home parks, small private water companies and HOA systems, and rural employers or private schools with their own wells. These are community and non-transient non-community systems, typically under 3,300 people. The owner is often an aging individual or family LLC with no operations staff.
problem: Owners face initial PFAS monitoring in 2027 and a 4.0 ppt limit still on the books. EPA's May 2026 proposal would move compliance from 2029 to 2031 and drop limits on four other compounds. The lead action level tightens on Nov 1, 2027. The whiplash freezes capex. Nobody at the business knows the sampling calendar, the accredited lab, the state portal, or the money ($1B of IIJA earmarked for PFAS testing and treatment, $7.2B of FY2026 SRF). The owner also cannot sell, because a first sample becomes a disclosure.
solution: Wedge: a $1,500 flat 'PFAS-2027 Readiness Pack' covering the sampling plan, lab coordination, result interpretation against 4.0 ppt, state filing and an options memo (treat, interconnect, drill, or sell). Upsell to a $600/mo retainer for the sampling calendar, consumer confidence report, lead inventory, monthly operator logs, tenant submetered billing and bookkeeping for a segregated water fund. The operator-of-record role is subcontracted to a state-certified operator partner. Later, broker and operate systems whose owners want out.
why_now: EPA's May 2026 proposals to delay PFAS compliance and rescind four limits have left small owners paralyzed, while 2027 initial monitoring still stands. Public money is earmarked: $1B IIJA for PFAS, $7.2B FY2026 SRF, and states are pushing consolidation of non-viable systems. The Boomer ownership wave is hitting the same long tail of tiny systems. EPA's science office was eliminated in 2026, so owners get less federal guidance.
revenue_model: $1,500 Readiness Pack. $400-$900/mo retainer per system by size. 6% success fee on SRF or state grants won. 2-4% brokerage fee on systems sold, plus an option to acquire orphan systems at distressed multiples using consolidation money.
non_obvious_insight: Federal delay does not remove the liability that appears at the first sample. Once a 2027 result exists it becomes a disclosure item in any sale, loan or insurance renewal. So the smart small owner samples early and under a plan. The firm that holds the compliance record becomes the natural buyer of last resort for a long tail of systems too small for the big acquirers. The retainer is the cheapest way to source those succession deals.
first_30_days: Sign one retired state-certified operator as partner and one accredited PFAS lab for a bulk rate. Join two state manufactured-housing associations and the state rural water association. Run free 'is my system covered?' webinars. Sell 10 Readiness Packs at $1,500 in one state, and use the results to prep 3 grant applications. Start compliance-only and add operator-of-record after the partner clears state rules.

title: ILIT Rescue After the Estate-Tax Cliff Disappeared
one_liner: A paid, documented review of irrevocable life insurance trusts built to pay estate tax that most families will never owe.
customer: Trustees (individuals and bank or trust companies), estate attorneys, and families holding ILITs with policies of $1M-$25M.
problem: For decades planners sold ILITs to fund federal estate tax. With the reported $15M-per-person exemption from 2026 (verify), many of these families will never owe it. Trusts keep paying premiums on policies that may be unnecessary, underfunded or poorly performing. Trustees fear fiduciary liability for doing nothing, yet nobody is paid to run the review.
solution: A 'trust-policy triage' service. Ingest the trust document and in-force illustration, classify the trust's purpose, and produce a decision memo: keep, reduce, 1035-exchange, sell, decant or terminate. It documents a prudent-process file for the trustee. Then execute through licensed partners (settlement broker, insurance agency, trust counsel).
why_now: The 2025 tax law reportedly raised and indexed the exclusion. About 10M life policies lapse per year (per the brief's cited market data), and the life-settlement market has active buyers (Coventry, Abacus). Wealth flows to heirs are large enough that leaving policy value on the table is now visible.
revenue_model: $2,500-$7,500 review fee per trust plus success fees on settled or exchanged policies where licensing allows.
non_obvious_insight: Fiduciary duty turns optimization into a mandatory review: trustees are exposed if they do nothing, so someone must be paid to produce the file even when the answer is 'keep'.
first_30_days: Recruit 2 estate attorneys and a licensed life-settlement broker. Pitch corporate trustees' special-assets desks. Run 10 reviews at a $1,500 intro price and learn which outcomes come up most.

title: Shelf Zero: Unclaimed Cremains Clearance Service
one_liner: A done-for-you compliance service that legally and respectfully empties the closet of unclaimed ashes that nearly every funeral home and crematory is afraid to touch.
customer: Independent funeral homes and crematories, where the owner or office manager pays per container. Secondary buyers are county public administrators and medical examiner offices. A third group is owners preparing to sell, whose buyers will flag the shelf in diligence.
problem: Cremation is now the majority disposition and still climbing. Families ghost after the cremation: an unpaid balance, an estrangement, a move, or a death of the only relative. State law on unclaimed remains varies widely. Search results show, for example, 120 days after written notice in Minnesota, at least 121 days in Texas, 60 days in Ohio and Nebraska, and 90 days with cemetery-contract rules in California. Directors won't scatter anything without a bulletproof paper trail, because one angry cousin surfacing four years later is a lawsuit or a board complaint. So the boxes pile up. A two-generation-old home can have dozens or hundreds, and staff feel guilt every time they walk past the shelf.
solution: A per-state playbook run as a service. Intake is a spreadsheet upload of name, date, contract and contact. Then skip-tracing for next of kin and authorizing agents, certified-mail and email notices on the statutory timeline, and a timestamped evidence file. Lawful disposition follows, through partner columbarium common niches, scattering gardens or sea scattering, each with a signed Certificate of Lawful Disposition per box. Veterans are identified through records requests and routed to the free national-cemetery inurnment route and Missing in America Project-type volunteers. Families who surface late can still reclaim through the funeral home for a small fee. An ongoing alert that flags containers at day 30, 60 and 90 stops the shelf refilling.
why_now: Cremation share keeps rising and household budgets are stretched, so abandonment is increasing. Consolidators such as SCI keep buying independents (about 22 funeral homes and 2 cemeteries for roughly $101M in 2025 per its filings). Their diligence treats an uncleared shelf as a liability, so retiring third-generation owners suddenly need a clean inventory. Skip-tracing and document automation are now cheap enough to run per box at a profit.
revenue_model: $175-$400 per container, tiered by state notice complexity. A $1,500-$3,000 pre-sale shelf audit and clearance bundle sells to owners about to list. A $49-$99/month ongoing aging-alert subscription covers new cases. Disposition partner fees (niche, scattering, transport) are passed through with a margin.
non_obvious_insight: The problem isn't the ashes, it's the paper trail. Nobody wants to be the person who scattered too early, so the shelf grows for decades. Outsiders assume it's a handful of boxes and a sad footnote. Inside, it's a compounding legal and emotional liability that every owner would pay a flat fee to make disappear, and the product being sold is really indemnifying documentation plus dignity, not disposal logistics.
first_30_days: Pick Ohio, Minnesota and Texas, where statutory safe harbors are clearest. Pay a funeral-law attorney a few thousand dollars to draft the three state notice templates and the disposition certificate. Offer a free 'shelf audit' to 30 homes via the state funeral directors' association newsletter and the private director Facebook groups. Convert five homes at $250 per box as pilots. Sign one local columbarium or church for a common-niche arrangement and one veterans-remains volunteer chapter.

title: Retiree Remote-Assist Bench for Robot Fleets
one_liner: A certified, US-based, part-time pool of retirees (ex-truckers, dispatchers, yard hands) who resolve robot and AV exceptions, billed by the assisted hour to fleet operators.
customer: Operators of driverless trucks, yard-automation systems, delivery robots and warehouse fleets (Bot Auto, Gatik, YardFlow-style deployments, sidewalk-robot firms), paying $45-65 per assisted hour.
problem: Every fleet needs remote humans for edge cases. Waymo alone runs about 70 agents on shift, partly in the Philippines, and offshore assist is now a political and first-responder question (NHTSA letter, Jul 2026). Meanwhile 65+ workers want flexible seated income and have the domain judgment, for example reading a truck yard or a weigh station.
solution: Recruit and train retirees on a common exception-handling curriculum. Certify them per vehicle or robot type. Supply them as a managed bench with scheduling, QA and a US-based, background-checked compliance story. Retirees earn $28-40 an hour for 10-20 hours a week, which keeps them under Social Security earnings limits.
why_now: Driverless freight went early-commercial in 2026 (Aurora about 200 trucks, Gatik 85k orders). Fleets are scaling remote-assist headcount, and regulators are scrutinizing where it sits.
revenue_model: Managed-service margin: bill $45-65 per hour, pay $28-40, keep about 35% gross margin. Add training and certification fees per operator.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input for autonomy is not more compute. It is cheap, trustworthy human judgment on demand. The demographic everyone treats as a care burden is the best-matched supply of that judgment.
first_30_days: Pitch two mid-size operators for a paid pilot in one metro (freight yards, sidewalk robots). Recruit 25 retired CDL drivers and dispatchers via trucker associations and AARP groups. Run a two-week training and bill the pilot at cost-plus.

title: Agent-Access Terms Index for Enterprises
one_liner: A living database and alert feed of what the top 500 SaaS and data vendors allow, meter and prohibit when your AI agents touch their APIs and data.
customer: General counsel, procurement and IT platform leads at 100-5,000 employee companies deploying agents, plus their outside counsel. SaaS vendors are a later customer.
problem: Most insiders read the Ninth Circuit ruling (the user, not the agent vendor, accessed Amazon) as 'agents can roam free'. For enterprises it means the fight moves to contract, and the user's company is the bound party. Vendors are already moving. SAP restricts third-party AI agent access to its APIs, Slack has throttled non-Marketplace apps and banned persistent indexes, and ServiceNow throttles inbound agent traffic. Vendors are also adding agent-action meters. No one tracks any of this, so a company can breach terms at a dozen vendors and learn about it from a suspension or audit letter.
solution: Build a structured agent-use rights matrix for about 500 vendors: allowed, banned or priced, rate limits, indexing, retention and training clauses, and official connector alternatives. Add change detection on terms and API policy pages with plain-English diffs. Add a connector that maps your OAuth-connected apps and agent inventory to the matrix and flags conflicts. Include a clause library, negotiation playbooks and an audit-defense pack.
why_now: Platform lockdowns (SAP, Slack, ServiceNow) and per-agent-action pricing arrived in 2025-26, and the Ninth Circuit ruling (August 2026) made contract the main battleground. Amazon can still seek rehearing, which adds uncertainty buyers want tracked.
revenue_model: $1.5-5k/month subscriptions for legal and procurement teams, $8-25k fixed-fee exposure reviews and negotiation packages, and later vendor-side benchmarking.
non_obvious_insight: Contract terms are becoming the price list and permission system of the agent economy, and they sit in unstructured legalese nobody indexes. The index is also the negotiating leverage, because it shows a buyer what comparable vendors concede.
first_30_days: Have an LLM plus a contract lawyer parse the terms and API policies of the top 100 SaaS vendors. Publish a free Agent Rights Scorecard for 25 of them to generate inbound. Sign 5 design partners at $1.5k/month and offer a $8-15k agent contract exposure review.

title: Provably Anonymous, Provably Employee Whistleblower Channel
one_liner: A reporting channel where a worker proves they hold a company email using zero-knowledge proofs, without the employer or vendor ever learning who they are.
customer: EU and UK employers with 50-500 staff that must run internal reporting channels, employment-law and compliance firms that deploy them, and works councils.
problem: Whistleblower-directive compliance is often a checkbox. Employees do not believe 'anonymous' hotlines that log IPs and identities, so use is low. Employers get junk or spoofed reports and cannot confirm that a reporter is a real current employee.
solution: ZK-email proofs of an employer-domain, DKIM-signed message let a reporter prove employment without revealing which mailbox. Per-report nullifiers block duplicates, and no identity is stored. Add anonymous two-way messaging, evidence upload, and a 'verified current employee in a group of at least 10' signal to the company. Independent cryptographic review is published.
why_now: ZK-email tooling is open source and maturing, EU digital-identity wallets are due by end 2026, and deepfake and spoofed reports are increasing. Whistleblower rules now apply to smaller firms, so many companies are buying cheap channels for the first time.
revenue_model: EUR 300-1,500 per month per company, with a 30% channel margin for law firms and a free tier for firms under 50 staff.
non_obvious_insight: Hotline usage is limited by trust in anonymity, which promises cannot improve, only making identification cryptographically impossible can. The same proof gives employers what they want (verified employee) and gives hostile insiders nothing.
first_30_days: Prototype with open-source zk-email libraries. Line up three employment-law firms and 10 SMEs for a free pilot, and commission a small third-party cryptography review to publish.

title: Lifeboat for Students of Closing Colleges
one_liner: A transfer-rescue service that maps every credit of a closing college's students into a receiving school's degree requirements, paid flat-fee by institutions and states, free to students.
customer: Payers: closing or distressed private colleges (which must file teach-out plans), state higher-ed agencies and accreditors, and regional receiving colleges that want transfer enrollment. Users: students at the closing school, roughly 500 to 3,000 per small college.
problem: When a small college closes, teach-out deals are improvised. Nursing, education and arts credits often fail to map. Students face a murky choice, because entering a teach-out forfeits closed-school loan discharge. Transcripts become hard to get, and many students simply stop out. One tally counts nine college closures in 2026, and Philadelphia Fed modeling points to dozens more.
solution: Within a week of an announced closure, ingest the catalog, syllabi and transcripts into a credit-mapping engine and produce course-by-course equivalency offers from 3 to 5 receiving schools. Give each student a lifeboat file: credits accepted, remaining requirements, time to degree, net price, and the teach-out versus transfer versus loan-discharge tradeoff, in plain language. Add written articulation letters from receiving schools, warm handoffs to admissions, and transcript custody. Offer a paid advocacy tier for credit-denial appeals.
why_now: The US high-school graduating class peaked in 2025 (about 3.9M) and shrinks about 13% by 2041, so the tuition-dependent-college shakeout is just starting. LLMs can now match syllabi to course equivalencies in hours, work that used to take registrars weeks per student. Receiving schools are hungry for transfer enrollment and closing schools have no bandwidth.
revenue_model: Flat fees only: a closure-response engagement ($25k to $75k) paid by the closing school, its state agency or a consortium; an annual credit-mapping and closure-readiness subscription ($30k to $100k) from receiving colleges; and a $149 to $299 student advocacy add-on. Do not charge per enrolled student, because the Higher Education Act's incentive-compensation ban prohibits enrollment bounties at Title IV schools (confirm with counsel).
non_obvious_insight: Students at a closing college are the highest-intent, highest-credit leads in higher education, but the bounty model that would normally monetize them is illegal, so the business must be paid for labor and neutrality instead. The moat is a growing corpus of verified course equivalencies plus being the trusted neutral on day one of a closure. Accreditors and state agencies need a vendor for teach-out compliance and do not want to be seen picking winners among rival colleges.
first_30_days: Build a tracker of announced and at-risk closures from accreditor notices and news. Pick the two nearest announced closures and offer their registrars and the state higher-ed agency a free pilot for one program (nursing or education). Line up 3 nearby receiving colleges' transfer directors. Hand-run LLM-assisted credit mapping on 50 students with a contract registrar reviewing, and deliver personal lifeboat files. Close the first flat-fee pilot with a receiving college or state agency, and publish a 'What to do when your college closes' guide for inbound.

title: Owner-Download: Capture Tacit Knowledge Before Sale
one_liner: Passively capture 60-90 days of an owner's calls, messages and jobs into a transferable playbook and a question-answering agent for the buyer.
customer: Owners aged 58+ of owner-dependent service and professional businesses ($300k-3M revenue) planning a sale in 12-36 months, plus the brokers who list them and the buyers who acquire them.
problem: Buyers discount hard for key-person dependency. The knowledge sits in the owner's head and phone: pricing instincts, customer quirks, vendor favors, unwritten rules. The traditional six-month handover rarely captures it.
solution: With consent, capture call recordings, texts and email, invoices, calendar and short weekly AI interviews. Produce SOPs, customer memory cards, learned pricing and quote logic, vendor scorecards and 'if X breaks, do Y' runbooks. The buyer gets a Q&A agent for year one ('how did the owner price gutters over 40 feet?') and the package goes in the data room as a transferable asset.
why_now: Long-context models, cheap call transcription and agentic retrieval make passive capture practical. Loosened SBA financing (up to $10M combined from July 2026) is drawing more first-time buyers who need this.
revenue_model: $2,500-6,000 per owner, broker referral fees, and a $199/month buyer subscription to the Q&A agent for 12 months.
non_obvious_insight: AI did not make this possible by automating the work but by making capture passive, so an owner no longer has to stop working to write manuals. Key-person discount is measurable, so the package can be priced against it.
first_30_days: Recruit five owners through two brokers in one vertical (HVAC, plumbing or landscaping). Run the capture pilots and ask buyers to rate the packages against a control listing on confidence and price.

title: Turnkey Six-Bed Care Homes for Nurse-Operators
one_liner: A licensing-and-operations platform that turns ordinary houses into small licensed residential care homes run by nurses and experienced aides.
customer: Nurses, CNAs and senior aides (including immigrant health workers) who want to own and run a home, plus small investors and families who own a suitable house.
problem: Insiders think the senior-housing gap ($275B, about 549k units by 2028) needs towers, REIT capital and 3-5 year development. Yet many states license 4-10 bed homes in normal single-family zoning. The barriers are licensing know-how, fire and ADA retrofits, staffing plans and a steady flow of admissions, not capital.
solution: A 90-day licensing sprint: zoning and state licensing packet, retrofit checklist, insurance, policies and procedures. Then staffing playbooks (1:3 to 1:6 ratios), charting, medication and compliance software, an admissions pipeline from hospital discharge planners who can't find beds, and financing partners (HELOC, sale-leaseback, small-investor pools). Start with states that have small-home license categories (for example Washington adult family homes, Arizona assisted-living homes and California small RCFEs).
why_now: Occupancy is at 90.1%, the highest since 2007. Inventory growth was 0.4% in Q1 2026, the lowest on record, and nothing new arrives before 2030. Hospital discharge teams are desperate for beds, and seniors hold a record $14.92T in home equity.
revenue_model: $6-12k onboarding fee per home, 5-8% management or software fee on revenue, and a placement fee from families where permitted. Later a captive group-purchasing and insurance program.
non_obvious_insight: Supply can appear in 6 months if the constraint is permission and playbooks, not concrete. One nurse-operator with a 5-bedroom house at $5-7k per resident per month can rival a mid-size facility's per-bed economics with no construction.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 prospective operators through nursing-school and CNA Facebook groups. Sell a $2,500 feasibility-and-licensing sprint, publish a 'how to license a six-bed home in [state]' guide as lead-gen, and line up one hospital discharge planner as a first referral source.

title: Inherited Low-Rate Mortgage Concierge for Heirs
one_liner: A flat-fee service that helps heirs keep, assume or transfer a parent's low-rate mortgage instead of paying it off at closing, and values that rate as an estate asset so siblings can buy each other out fairly.
customer: Heirs (Gen X, aged 45-60) who inherit a home with a mortgage at 3-4% while new loans cost about 7.5%. The estate attorneys, probate realtors and bank trust officers who advise them refer clients and pay for tooling.
problem: The default estate path is to sell the house and pay off the loan, which destroys below-market financing. On a $300K balance at about 3.25% with 22 years left versus 7.5%, the rate is worth roughly $90K in present value (my calculation). Federal rules generally bar lenders from calling loans due on transfer to relatives at death, and confirmed successors have servicing rights under CFPB rules, but servicers are slow and inconsistent and heirs do not know. Siblings often cannot buy each other out at current rates, and a buyer's market with concessions on 44.7% of sales makes forced sales costlier.
solution: Within days of a death, verify loan type, rate, balance and assumability and confirm successor-in-interest status with the servicer. Bridge payments during probate, and produce a Rate Asset Report that values the rate for the estate inventory so heirs can split fairly. Structure buyouts with junior notes or partner lenders so one heir keeps or rents the house, and for sellers show where FHA or VA assumability lifts the sale price. Confirm applicability with counsel, since protections generally cover owner-occupied 1-4 unit homes.
why_now: Rates are rising again (Redfin: futures price the Fed funds rate at 5% by end-2027, and the 30-year is about 7.4-7.6%). A large share of Boomer mortgages sit below 4%, and the first wave of the transfer is arriving. Record concessions make selling into this market expensive. ROAD to Housing Act limits on institutional single-family owners push heirs to be small landlords.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 flat fee per estate or a share of rate-value preserved, a $499 Rate Asset Report, referral fees from buyout lenders, and $200 per month tooling subscriptions for probate attorneys.
non_obvious_insight: The great wealth transfer is counted in balance-sheet dollars, but in a 7.5% world the most valuable asset in many middle-class estates is the interest rate on the parent's mortgage, and the default estate process throws it away at closing.
first_30_days: Write servicer letter templates and an assumability checklist reviewed by an attorney. Recruit five probate attorneys and three probate realtors. Launch the $499 Rate Asset Report to estates with mortgages and track how many convert to the full service. Sign one HELOC or non-QM lender as buyout-financing partner.

title: Employer-Backed Block Leases for Hourly Workers
one_liner: A broker that packages 20-100 unit block leases in concession-heavy buildings, backed by an employer's credit guarantee and payroll deduction, to cut rent for hourly workers without raising wages.
customer: Hospital systems, school districts, hotels, casinos and retailers with recruiting and turnover pain, paired with owners of lease-up and high-concession properties who pay the placement fee.
problem: A typical retail worker earns $34,436 against $71,172 needed for a typical $1,779 apartment. Employers lose workers to housing costs, while owners in lease-up hand out 15-37% concessions to anonymous renters and carry 34 days of vacancy.
solution: Negotiate discounted block rents in exchange for guaranteed occupancy. The employer provides a credit guarantee rather than a subsidy, plus optional payroll deduction, and we run eligibility, lease templates, guarantee underwriting and monitoring. The tenant's discount is funded by the owner's savings on concessions, marketing, vacancy and turnover.
why_now: The rental glut and record concessions give owners a reason to trade price for certainty. Employer labor tightness is high, and traditional locators ignore blocks because commissions are small.
revenue_model: Owner-paid placement fee of 3-4% of first-year rent, employer platform fee of $8-15 per enrolled unit per month, and an optional guarantee premium.
non_obvious_insight: The landlord is buying occupancy certainty, not tenants, and avoided concession, vacancy and turnover can approach 10-15% of annual rent, more than a free month per tenant. Employers can create affordability by lending credit instead of paying wages, which also helps them avoid taxable-benefit complications.
first_30_days: Pick Austin or Atlanta. Get three owners with 300+ unit lease-ups to sign a 10%-off block-lease term sheet. Pitch five HR or recruiting heads at hospital and community-college systems. Run one 25-unit pilot and collect the placement fee.

title: Escrow Shock Early Warning for Servicers
one_liner: Soft reinsurance produces homeowner nonrenewals, which produce force-placed cover and escrow shortages, which produce delinquencies on servicers' books. Predict and defuse the shock before it lands.
customer: Mid-size mortgage servicers (50k-1M loans), including non-bank and credit-union servicers with loss-mitigation and hazard-insurance teams.
problem: Homeowner insurance now rivals mortgage payments (Tacoma News Tribune, Aug 2026). Nonrenewals hit records (Utah highest in 2025, New Mexico a record 6,200, county rate spikes up to 33% in H1 2026). When coverage lapses or moves to a FAIR plan, escrow analyses jump payments by hundreds of dollars a month and delinquencies follow.
solution: Score every loan for escrow-shock risk 90 days out, using state nonrenewal patterns, filed rate changes, tax data and the servicer's own hazard-insurance tracking. Then run assisted outreach before the shortage letter goes out: re-shop with an agent network, mitigation credits, and payment-plan options. Deliver dashboards and borrower-level outcomes to loss-mitigation heads.
why_now: Record nonrenewals, California's FAIR Plan taking more new loans (beinsure, Aug 2026), a HELOC surge signaling stretched households, and the household credit stress in the brief (record auto delinquencies, K-shaped economy).
revenue_model: $75-$200 per borrower resolved, or $0.50-$1.00 per loan per year SaaS. Optional share of avoided force-placed premium.
non_obvious_insight: Servicers treat insurance as lapse-tracking compliance, not delinquency prevention. A single loss-mitigation case can cost hundreds of dollars, so even a 1% reduction in shock-driven delinquency pays for the product. Target servicers with investor and regulator pressure, since some earn money on force-placed cover.
first_30_days: Build a free escrow-shock heat map for three states from public data as a lead magnet. Cold-outreach loss-mitigation heads at 30 mid-size and credit-union servicers, and sign one pilot on about 20k loans.

title: Neutral Legacy Animal-Data Vault for NAM Validation
one_liner: A neutral data trust that turns pharma's shelved animal-study results into blinded concordance benchmarks organoid and organ-chip makers use to prove their methods are 'adequately validated.'
customer: Organoid, organ-chip and other NAM startups needing FDA-credible validation, CROs, and pharma tox groups that contribute data and earn credits.
problem: FDA's Sept 21, 2026 direct final rule swapped 'animal tests' for 'nonclinical tests' but requires methods to be 'adequately validated'. Its NAM use-case database has only 25 entries. Validation needs ground truth: in vivo and clinical outcomes for many compounds. That lives in competing pharma archives and old PDFs, and pharma cannot pool proprietary data across competitors.
solution: Contributors deposit outcomes for shelved or dead compounds (species, dose, target-organ findings, human outcome where known) into a trust with blinded, query-only access. NAM developers submit predictions on a blinded panel of 100-200 compounds. They receive sensitivity, specificity and PPV by context of use, in a format built for FDA meetings. Contributors earn free validation credits. Start from public sources: FDA and EMA review documents, NTP, open toxicogenomics sets and DILI ranking lists.
why_now: The FDA rule landed this week and the NAM database is thin. NIH turbulence pushes toward cheaper methods. The IMI eTOX project pooled 8,196 studies on 1,947 compounds from 13 pharma companies, which proves the sharing model can work, but it was a research consortium and not a validation product.
revenue_model: $20-100k per validation report, annual memberships ($50-150k for NAM vendors; $100k or in-kind data for pharma), and licensing of benchmark panels to CROs.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone treats animal data as obsolete. As new animal studies decline, the historical archive becomes a fixed, non-renewable supply and the only ground truth for validating replacements. Dead compounds carry no competitive risk, so the usual objection to sharing disappears. The owner of the concordance yardstick becomes a toll-taker on every NAM filing.
first_30_days: Assemble a public 150-compound reference set with animal and human outcomes. Sell 3-5 'pre-validation concordance reports' at $10-20k to organ-chip and organoid startups. Interview 5 pharma tox heads about pilot contributions of 20-50 shelved compounds each. Recruit a former FDA nonclinical reviewer as an advisor.
